rules.Rule: Total NEWS2 score of 7 or more
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Total NEWS2 ≥ 7 on the latest complete set of observations.
rules.Data needed: All 7 NEWS2 parameters: heart rate, respiratory rate, SpO2, systolic BP, temperature, level of consciousness, supplemental oxygen yes/no (hr, rr, spo2, sbp, temp, alert, on_oxygen)
rules.What to do now: Alert the crew medical officer (CMO) now and start continuous vital-sign monitoring. Send the Earth packet immediately and bring the emergency medical kit.
rules.Why (rationale): NEWS2 is the standard early warning score of the UK National Health Service for detecting acute deterioration in adults. According to the official chart (RCP 2017, Chart 2), a total of 7 or more is high risk and calls for an urgent or emergency response by a team with airway management skills. NICE recommends recalculating every 30 minutes at high risk. In 251,266 hospital admissions, NEWS2 discriminated death within 24 hours with an AUROC of 0.89 in patients not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (Pimentel 2019).
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_CH2); Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_RCP); Pimentel MAF (PIMENTEL2019); Smith GB (SMITH2013); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE)
rules.Type of evidence: International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Validated in hospitalised adults on Earth, not in astronauts. In microgravity, baseline heart rate and blood pressure change because of fluid redistribution; this is why the score is complemented by the personal baseline rule (R04).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Total NEWS2 of 5 or 6.
rules.What to do now: CMO assessment within 1 hour. Recheck vital signs at least every hour, look for a cause (infection, pain, dehydration) and consult Earth at the next link.
rules.Why (rationale): In NEWS2, a score of 5–6 is medium risk and the 'key threshold for an urgent response' (RCP 2017, Chart 2). NICE classifies 5–6 as moderate risk of severe illness or death from sepsis and recommends recalculating every hour.
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_CH2); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The 1-hour window is our adaptation to the spacecraft; in hospital the response is provided by a clinical team.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: A single vital sign scoring 3 points
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Any individual NEWS2 parameter scoring 3 points (e.g., RR ≤ 8 or ≥ 25; SpO2 ≤ 91%; SBP ≤ 90 or ≥ 220; HR ≤ 40 or ≥ 131; new confusion; T ≤ 35.0 °C), even if the total is below 5.
rules.What to do now: Repeat the abnormal measurement first. If confirmed, the CMO reviews it within 1 hour and vital signs are rechecked every hour.
rules.Why (rationale): NEWS2 calls a parameter scoring 3 a 'red score': low-to-medium risk that requires an urgent response (RCP 2017, Chart 2). NICE recommends a high-priority review by a competent clinician.
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_CH2); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Repeating the measurement avoids false alarms caused by artefacts (movement, a loose sensor).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): NEWS2 rises by 2 or more points from the crewmember's baseline mean, or heart rate, respiratory rate or temperature reaches a z-score ≥ 3 on 2 consecutive measurements, even if the total is below 5.
rules.Data needed: Current vital signs + baseline (days 1–7): hr_z, rr_z, temp_z
rules.What to do now: Recheck vital signs in 1 hour and complete a symptom check-in. If the change persists, the CMO reviews it today.
rules.Why (rationale): NEWS2 stresses monitoring the trend of the score, not just a single value, and NICE recommends recalculating and reassessing after any unexpected change (section 1.6.6). Astronauts are healthy adults whose baseline sits far from the NEWS2 cut-offs, so a large change for that person can go unnoticed with the general score.
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_RCP); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The '+2 points' and 'z ≥ 3' cut-offs are our own design choices and have not been validated. They must be presented as exploratory.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): New pain, pressure, tightness or burning in the chest, shoulder, arm, neck, jaw or upper abdomen, not explained by trauma.
rules.What to do now: Stop activity and rest. Unless allergic to aspirin, actively bleeding, or the pain is tearing and goes to the back, chew 162–325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin from the medical kit. Record a 12-lead ECG if available and vital signs every 5 minutes; alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The 2021 AHA/ACC guideline recommends replacing 'typical/atypical' with 'cardiac, possibly cardiac or noncardiac', notes that pain may be felt in the shoulder, arm, neck, jaw or epigastrium, and calls for expedited evaluation of acute chest pain. An ECG should be obtained promptly (within 10 minutes in emergency settings). Women more often also report nausea, palpitations or shortness of breath. The ISS carries a defibrillator and an advanced life support pack (NASA 2011).
rules.Sources (short citation): Gulati M (GULATI2021); Rao SV (RAO2025); Anderson JL (ACCAHA2007); American Family Physician (AAFP2023); Hailey M (NASA_HMS)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline; Peer-reviewed journal
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Many causes are not cardiac; we accept overtriage. Aspirin: ACC/AHA guidelines (2007, class I, for prehospital services) recommend 162–325 mg chewed for suspected acute coronary syndrome, and the 2025 guideline retains the aspirin loading dose. It is withheld in case of allergy, active bleeding or tearing pain radiating to the back (suspected aortic dissection). It must be confirmed that the mission medical kit includes aspirin.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): New shortness of breath at rest, or RR ≥ 25/min, or SpO2 ≤ 91%.
rules.Data needed: dyspnea = yes, or rr, or spo2
rules.What to do now: Stop activity and sit upright. Give oxygen only if SpO2 is below 94 %, aiming for 94–98 %; alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The British Thoracic Society oxygen guideline states that oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness, and sets a target SpO2 of 94–98% for most acutely ill patients. RR ≥ 25 and SpO2 ≤ 91% are the 3-point values in NEWS2. Thrombosis is a real risk in flight: stagnant or reversed jugular venous flow and thrombi were found in 11 astronauts (JAMA Netw Open 2019), and a case of jugular thrombosis treated on the ISS has been published (NEJM 2020).
rules.Sources (short citation): O'Driscoll BR (BTS2017); Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_CH2); Marshall-Goebel K (MARSHALL2019); Auñón-Chancellor SM (AUNON2020)
rules.Type of evidence: International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The 88–92% target for patients at risk of hypercapnia (COPD) does not apply to healthy astronauts.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Sudden onset of any of the following: loss of balance, visual disturbance, facial droop, arm or leg weakness, or difficulty speaking (BE-FAST).
rules.What to do now: Note the exact time the crewmember was last seen normal. Check blood glucose, keep them at rest, and alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): BE-FAST adds Balance and Eyes to FAST and reduces the proportion of missed strokes (Stroke 2017). Under the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline, thrombolysis should start as early as possible within 4.5 hours of onset, which is why recording the exact time matters. Blood glucose rules out hypoglycaemia mimicking a stroke; blood glucose can be measured on the ISS.
rules.Sources (short citation): Aroor S (AROOR2017); Prabhakaran S (AIS2026)
rules.Type of evidence: International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: There is no CT scanner or standard thrombolysis on the spacecraft; the rule enables rapid recognition and a joint decision with Earth.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Headache with at least one SNNOOP10 red flag: sudden onset (peak within 1 minute, 'worst headache of my life'), neurological deficit or confusion, fever or neck stiffness, papilloedema or visual changes, triggered by exertion, coughing or Valsalva, progressive worsening or change in pattern.
rules.What to do now: Keep the crewmember at rest, run the BE-FAST check and full vital signs, and alert the CMO and Earth now. Do not give new medication until the CMO reviews.
rules.Why (rationale): SNNOOP10 (Neurology 2019) lists 15 red flags for secondary headache. Headache is very common in flight (22 of 24 astronauts), so these red flags are needed to separate benign from serious causes. Papilloedema and visual changes are especially relevant in space because of spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS).
rules.Sources (short citation): Do TP (SNNOOP10); van Oosterhout WPJ (VANOOST2024)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Red flags guide the assessment; they do not all have the same predictive value.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Severe abdominal pain or acute urinary problem
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Severe abdominal or flank pain (≥ 7/10) or lasting more than 6 hours, colicky pain radiating to the groin, blood in the urine with pain, or inability to pass urine despite the urge.
rules.What to do now: CMO examination within 1 hour. Nothing by mouth until reviewed; use ultrasound if available and consult Earth. If unable to urinate, the CMO follows the onboard catheter procedure.
rules.Why (rationale): According to NASA, kidney stones are the second most likely cause of medical evacuation from the ISS and urosepsis the third (IMM model). NASA has documented 9 cases of urinary retention in flight (16 including suggestive symptoms), 4.5 times more likely in women. Appendicitis is the most common abdominal surgical emergency and has an international guideline (WSES 2020).
rules.Sources (short citation): NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO) (NASA_URI); Di Saverio S (WSES2020)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The '≥ 7/10' and '6 hours' cut-offs are design choices. If fever with NEWS2 ≥ 5 is also present, R11 or R11b takes precedence.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Transient loss of consciousness with any of: occurred during exertion or while lying down, palpitations immediately before, chest pain, shortness of breath, new abdominal pain or headache, no warning symptoms, or persistent SBP < 90 or HR < 40.
rules.What to do now: Keep the crewmember lying flat and restrained, check pulse and breathing, record an ECG if available, keep the defibrillator ready, and alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The 2018 European Society of Cardiology syncope guideline defines high-risk features that suggest a serious cause (arrhythmia or structural heart disease), such as syncope during exertion or while supine, preceding palpitations, new associated symptoms and persistent bradycardia below 40 bpm.
rules.Sources (short citation): Brignole M (ESC2018); Hailey M (NASA_HMS)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Syncope is rare in microgravity; the risk rises at landing and in lunar or Martian gravity (orthostatic intolerance).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Syncope preceded by warning symptoms (feeling hot, nausea, pallor), after prolonged standing or after a meal, with none of the R10 features.
rules.What to do now: Lie down and drink fluids. The CMO reviews within 1 hour with an ECG and lying/standing vital signs if possible.
rules.Why (rationale): The 2018 ESC guideline states that low-risk patients usually have reflex syncope with an excellent prognosis, but they still warrant evaluation with an ECG.
rules.Sources (short citation): Brignole M (ESC2018)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Variant added so that rule R10 does not leave cases without a level.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Fever with NEWS2 of 7 or more (probable sepsis)
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Temperature ≥ 38.1 °C (or ≤ 36.0 °C) with suspected infection and NEWS2 ≥ 7.
rules.What to do now: Treat as probable sepsis: CMO review now, look for the source (urine, lungs, skin), and start antibiotics per the onboard protocol within 1 hour. Consult Earth now and recheck NEWS2 every 30 minutes.
rules.Why (rationale): NICE NG253 (rec. 1.6.2) classifies NEWS2 ≥ 7 as high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis and recommends recalculating every 30 minutes (1.6.5). The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 recommends giving antimicrobials immediately, ideally within the first hour, when sepsis is probable or shock is present. According to NASA, urosepsis is one of the most likely causes of evacuation from the ISS.
rules.Sources (short citation): Evans L (SSC2021); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE); NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO) (NASA_URI)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Validated in hospitals on Earth; on the spacecraft the available antibiotic depends on the medical kit.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Fever with NEWS2 of 5 or 6 (possible sepsis)
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Temperature ≥ 38.1 °C (or ≤ 36.0 °C) with suspected infection and NEWS2 of 5 or 6.
rules.What to do now: CMO review within 1 hour; look for the source and recheck NEWS2 every hour. If concern for infection persists, start antibiotics per the onboard protocol within 3 hours. Escalate to EMERGENCY at once if NEWS2 reaches 7.
rules.Why (rationale): NICE NG253 (recs. 1.6.2 and 1.6.5) classifies NEWS2 of 5–6 as moderate risk and recommends recalculating every hour. For possible sepsis without shock, the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 suggests a rapid assessment and antimicrobials within 3 hours if concern for infection persists.
rules.Sources (short citation): National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE); Evans L (SSC2021)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Decision based on the guidelines (previously EMERGENCY because of the spacecraft's isolation). If the crew cannot reassess every hour, it should be treated as EMERGENCY.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Sudden loss of vision or double vision
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Sudden total or partial loss of vision in one or both eyes, or new double vision.
rules.What to do now: Note the time of onset, check visual acuity in each eye and run BE-FAST; alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The AHA states that central retinal artery occlusion is a medical emergency equivalent to a stroke, with a treatment window of 4.5 hours from the first symptoms.
rules.Sources (short citation): Mac Grory B (MACGRORY2021); Prabhakaran S (AIS2026)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: There is no thrombolysis on the spacecraft; rapid recognition allows a joint decision with Earth.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Blurred near vision or gradual change in vision over days or weeks, painless and without other symptoms.
rules.What to do now: Record visual acuity and an Amsler grid test today, schedule an OCT or fundus exam, and send the results to Earth's eye specialist.
rules.Why (rationale): In the 2020 npj Microgravity review, about 15% of long-duration astronauts had clinically significant optic disc oedema and more than 20% had choroidal folds. The typical symptom is reduced near vision due to a hyperopic shift of +0.50 to +1.75 dioptres. The ISS has OCT, an Amsler grid, visual acuity testing and fundoscopy.
rules.Sources (short citation): Lee AG (LEE2020)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The 15% figure comes from a personal communication cited in the review; choroidal folds are published data.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Rash or skin lesion without red flags (includes cold sores)
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Rash, irritation or skin lesion (including cold sores) without fever, extensive blistering, lesions in the mouth or eyes, swelling of the lips or tongue, or shortness of breath.
rules.What to do now: Keep the area clean and dry, use the onboard topical treatment from the medical kit, take a photo and recheck in 48 hours. Report at once if fever, blisters, mouth or eye sores, or lip swelling appear.
rules.Why (rationale): Among 46 long-duration ISS crewmembers, rash or dermatitis was the most frequent symptom: 23 events, 1.12 per flight-year; cold sores occurred 0.3 times per flight-year (Crucian 2016). The red flags (swelling of the lips or tongue, breathing difficulty) follow the WAO 2020 anaphylaxis guidance and raise the level.
rules.Sources (short citation): Crucian B (CRUCIAN2016); Cardona V (WAO2020)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: These are reported symptoms, not confirmed diagnoses.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Congestion, rhinitis or sneezing without fever (≤ 38.0 °C), without severe facial pain and lasting less than 10 days.
rules.What to do now: Use the decongestant or saline from the medical kit and recheck in 72 hours. Report if fever, ear pain, or symptoms last more than 10 days.
rules.Why (rationale): Prolonged congestion was the second most frequent symptom on the ISS: 20 events, 0.97 per flight-year (Crucian 2016). The IDSA guideline suggests bacterial sinusitis if symptoms last more than 10 days without improvement, if there is high fever with facial pain, or if they worsen after initial improvement.
rules.Sources (short citation): Crucian B (CRUCIAN2016); Chow AW (IDSA2012)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: In flight, part of the congestion is due to the headward shift of body fluids.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Pressing, bilateral, mild-to-moderate headache without marked nausea, with no SNNOOP10 red flag, NEWS2 < 5 and normal CO2.
rules.What to do now: Rest, hydrate and take the onboard pain reliever per the medical kit. Check cabin CO2 and recheck in 4 hours; report if it worsens or any warning sign appears.
rules.Why (rationale): In a prospective study published in Neurology (2024), 22 of 24 astronauts (92%) had headache in flight versus 38% before flight; 90% of episodes were tension-type. The definition of tension-type headache follows the international classification ICHD-3.
rules.Sources (short citation): van Oosterhout WPJ (VANOOST2024); Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (ICHD3); NASA OCHMO (NASA_CO2)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Check CO2, because NASA associates headaches with levels of 2.8–4.5 mmHg.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): 3-minute PVT-B: lapses (> 355 ms) above the personal baseline (mean + 2 standard deviations), or median reaction time ≥ 10% slower than baseline.
rules.What to do now: Not fit for critical tasks right now: postpone the spacewalk or robotics task if possible, give a sleep opportunity, and repeat the test before the task.
rules.Why (rationale): The PVT-B lasts 3 minutes with inter-stimulus intervals of 1 to 4 seconds; with a lapse threshold of 355 ms it performs like the standard 10-minute PVT (Acta Astronautica 2011). It is the test used in the ISS Reaction Self Test. In 24 astronauts and 2,856 tests, sleeping less than 6 hours was associated with slower responses and more stress (Sleep 2022).
rules.Sources (short citation): Basner M (BASNER2011); Jones CW (JONES2022)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The '+2 SD' and '10%' cut-offs are design choices. Our browser version has not been validated (screen latency varies).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Slept less than 6 hours and KSS ≥ 7 ('sleepy') before a critical task.
rules.What to do now: Not fit for critical tasks today: reschedule the task if possible, allow a nap or sleep period, and repeat the KSS and reaction test before starting.
rules.Why (rationale): Astronauts sleep about 6 hours per night on average (6.09 h on the ISS) and three quarters used sleep medication (Lancet Neurology 2014). Sleeping < 6 h impairs performance (Sleep 2022). On the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, 7 means 'sleepy, but no effort to keep awake'; the scale has been validated against EEG and performance (Clin Neurophysiol 2006).
rules.Sources (short citation): Jones CW (JONES2022); Barger LK (BARGER2014); Åkerstedt T (AKERSTEDT1990); Kaida K (KAIDA2006)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The combination '< 6 h and KSS ≥ 7' is a design choice.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Mean CO2 over the last hour above 3 mmHg in the module.
rules.What to do now: Tell the flight engineer, check the CO2 removal system and air circulation, and move to a better-ventilated module if possible. Log any headache or fatigue.
rules.Why (rationale): Requirement NASA-STD-3001 [V2 6004] states: 'the system shall limit the 1-hour average CO2 partial pressure in the habitable volume to no more than 3 mmHg'. NASA also states that the 7-day average should be below 2.5 mmHg to keep the risk of headache below 1%, and associates headaches with 2.8–4.5 mmHg. On the ISS, each 1 mmHg increase was associated with a doubling of the odds of reported headache (Law 2014).
rules.Sources (short citation): NASA OCHMO (NASA_CO2); Law J (LAW2014); van Oosterhout WPJ (VANOOST2024)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; Q1 journal (high impact); Peer-reviewed journal
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The 2024 prospective study found no association between CO2 and headache. We state this openly in the pitch.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Any of the 7 NEWS2 parameters is missing and no red-flag rule has been triggered.
rules.What to do now: Measure the missing vital signs and run the evaluation again. If the crewmember feels unwell, call the CMO without waiting.
rules.Why (rationale): NEWS2 is valid only with all 7 parameters. It is better for the app to say 'I don't know' than to make up a level. The proportion of abstentions is reported in the evaluation.
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_RCP)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Design choice based on the correct use of NEWS2.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): SpO2 flagged as unreliable: poor signal or low perfusion according to the oximeter, cold hands, movement, or a normal SpO2 that does not match shortness of breath or a high respiratory rate.
rules.Data needed: spo2 + perfusion_index or device signal-quality flag
rules.What to do now: Warm the hand, use another finger, keep still and repeat. Do not trust a single normal reading if the crewmember looks unwell; use the other vital signs.
rules.Why (rationale): In Black patients, occult hypoxaemia (normal oximeter reading with low true oxygen saturation) was about 3 times as frequent as in White patients (NEJM 2020). The error grows at low saturation and with low perfusion in darker skin (Anesthesiology 2005; Gudelunas 2024). In 2025 the FDA proposed requiring oximeter testing across skin tones using the Monk scale.
rules.Sources (short citation): Sjoding MW (SJODING2020); Gudelunas MK (GUDELUNAS2024); Bickler PE (BICKLER2005); U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA2025)
rules.Type of evidence: Regulator (FDA); Q1 journal (high impact); Peer-reviewed journal
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: The 'low perfusion' threshold depends on the oximeter model: use the manufacturer's indicator.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: New confusion or reduced level of consciousness
rules.Trigger (if this happens): New confusion, disorientation or drowsiness (not responding normally), even without other vital signs.
rules.What to do now: Keep the crewmember safe and do not leave them alone. Check blood glucose and full vital signs, and alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): In NEWS2, new confusion alone scores 3 points (ACVPU scale) and requires an urgent response. It is one of the signs most strongly associated with serious illness (sepsis, stroke, hypoglycaemia, liver failure).
rules.Sources (short citation): Royal College of Physicians (NEWS2_RCP); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Without complete vital signs the app cannot calculate NEWS2, so confusion is treated as an independent red flag.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Swelling or pain of one leg (possible thrombosis)
rules.Trigger (if this happens): New swelling, pain or redness of one leg or arm, or of one side of the neck, not explained by trauma and without shortness of breath or chest pain (if present, R05/R06 take precedence).
rules.What to do now: Avoid exercise with that limb, measure both limbs, use ultrasound if available, and consult the CMO within 1 hour and Earth at the next link. Escalate at once if breathlessness or chest pain appears.
rules.Why (rationale): The American Society of Hematology guideline recommends assessing every suspected thrombosis with clinical probability and an imaging test (ultrasound). The risk in flight is documented: stagnant or reversed jugular flow and thrombi in astronauts (JAMA Netw Open 2019; NEJM 2020).
rules.Sources (short citation): Lim W (ASH2018); Marshall-Goebel K (MARSHALL2019); Auñón-Chancellor SM (AUNON2020)
rules.Type of evidence: International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Decided: PRIORITY. The benchmark classifies deep vein thrombosis as emergent, so KAWSAY will miss case S05; we accept this because the ASH guideline calls for diagnosis by ultrasound (not resuscitation), and the only thrombosis case on the ISS was managed on board with anticoagulation, without evacuation (Auñón-Chancellor 2020).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Abdominal pain with fever, rigid abdomen or persistent vomiting
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Abdominal pain with fever (≥ 38.0 °C measured or reported), a rigid or very tender abdomen, or vomiting that does not stop.
rules.What to do now: Nothing by mouth. CMO examination now, ultrasound if available, and consult Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The WSES 2020 appendicitis guideline uses pain with fever, abdominal guarding and vomiting as high-risk signs that require urgent assessment. This rule raises the level set by R09 when these signs are present.
rules.Sources (short citation): Di Saverio S (WSES2020); NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO) (NASA_URI)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: There is no surgery on the spacecraft; the rule supports a rapid decision with Earth (possible evacuation from low Earth orbit).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): After an allergen or with no clear cause: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, or dizziness with low blood pressure.
rules.What to do now: Follow the onboard anaphylaxis procedure immediately (epinephrine per medical kit), lay the crewmember flat, and alert the CMO and Earth now.
rules.Why (rationale): The World Allergy Organization anaphylaxis guidance (WAO 2020) defines these clinical criteria and calls for immediate treatment with adrenaline (epinephrine).
rules.Sources (short citation): Cardona V (WAO2020)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: A purely local reaction (for example, a sting with a swollen lip and no other signs) does not meet this rule.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): An area of red, warm, swollen and painful skin that is spreading, with or without fever.
rules.What to do now: Mark the edges of the red area with a pen, take a photo, and have the CMO review within 1 hour. Consult Earth about antibiotics per the onboard protocol.
rules.Why (rationale): The IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline (2014) describes cellulitis and recommends antibiotic treatment; marking the edge shows whether it is advancing. There were 6 skin infections in 20.6 flight-years on the ISS (Crucian 2016).
rules.Sources (short citation): Stevens DL (IDSA_SSTI2014); Crucian B (CRUCIAN2016)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: With fever and NEWS2 ≥ 5, R11 or R11b takes precedence (possible sepsis).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Vomiting or diarrhoea with risk of dehydration
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Vomiting or diarrhoea that prevents keeping fluids down, with blood in the stool, or with fever.
rules.What to do now: Start oral rehydration in small, frequent sips if tolerated, record intake and output, and have the CMO review within 1 hour.
rules.Why (rationale): The IDSA infectious diarrhoea guideline (2017) prioritises assessing dehydration and investigating bloody or febrile diarrhoea.
rules.Sources (short citation): Shane AL (IDSA_DIARR2017)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Mild diarrhoea that still allows drinking fluids is SELF-CARE.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Temperature ≥ 38.0 °C with no higher-level rule triggered and NEWS2 < 5 (or NEWS2 not available).
rules.What to do now: Rest, drink fluids, recheck temperature and vital signs every 4–6 hours, and have the CMO review within 24 hours. Escalate if new symptoms appear.
rules.Why (rationale): NICE considers a NEWS2 of 1–4 low risk but recommends reassessment every 4–6 hours. In flight the immune system is altered and infections are frequent (3.4 clinical events per flight-year), so fever is reviewed within 24 hours.
rules.Sources (short citation): National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (NICE); Crucian B (CRUCIAN2016)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Conservative design choice for the spacecraft; on Earth many viral fevers are managed with self-care.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Symptoms that do not improve or get worse
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Respiratory or other symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement, or worsening after initial improvement.
rules.What to do now: Schedule a CMO review within 24 hours and send a summary to Earth at the next link.
rules.Why (rationale): The IDSA rhinosinusitis guideline uses a duration of more than 10 days without improvement and worsening after initial improvement as criteria to suspect bacterial infection.
rules.Sources (short citation): Chow AW (IDSA2012)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Applying it outside the respiratory tract is a design choice.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Trigger (if this happens): Burning on urination, urgency or increased frequency, without fever, flank pain or retention.
rules.What to do now: Drink more fluids, test urine if a test strip is available, and have the CMO review within 24 hours. Escalate if fever or flank pain appears.
rules.Why (rationale): The international guideline on uncomplicated cystitis (IDSA/ESCMID) separates simple cystitis from pyelonephritis by the presence of fever and flank pain. NASA describes urinary tract infection as an in-flight risk, especially with catheter use.
rules.Sources (short citation): Gupta K (IDSA_UTI2011); NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO) (NASA_URI)
rules.Type of evidence: Official NASA document; International clinical guideline
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: With fever and NEWS2 ≥ 5, R11 or R11b takes precedence (possible urosepsis).
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Sore throat with fever and no cough
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Sore throat with fever ≥ 38.0 °C and no cough (with or without tonsillar exudate or swollen lymph nodes).
rules.Data needed: sore_throat = yes, fever = yes, cough = no
rules.What to do now: Rest and fluids; the CMO reviews within 24 hours and uses a rapid strep test if available.
rules.Why (rationale): The IDSA group A streptococcal pharyngitis guideline (2012) states that fever without cough, with exudate or swollen nodes, suggests streptococcal infection and warrants testing, whereas cough and cold symptoms suggest a viral cause.
rules.Sources (short citation): Shulman ST (IDSA_GAS2012)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: Without a rapid test on board, the antibiotic decision rests with the CMO and Earth.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

rules.Rule: Brief dizziness on head movement without neurological symptoms
rules.Trigger (if this happens): Vertigo lasting seconds to less than 1 minute, triggered by moving the head or lying down, without weakness, speech problems, double vision or severe headache.
rules.What to do now: Avoid sudden head movements and critical tasks while dizzy; the CMO reviews within 24 hours. Escalate at once if any BE-FAST sign appears.
rules.Why (rationale): The benign paroxysmal positional vertigo guideline (AAO-HNS 2017) describes it as brief episodes triggered by head position, without other neurological signs. If neurological signs are present, R07 takes precedence (possible stroke).
rules.Sources (short citation): Bhattacharyya N (BPPV2017); Aroor S (AROOR2017)
rules.Type of evidence: International clinical guideline; Q1 journal (high impact)
rules.Limitations / what to disclose: In flight and after returning to gravity, dizziness may be due to vestibular adaptation.
rules.Reviewed by: Evidence-based decisions applied (see sheet 'Data origin & decisions'); pending physician sign-off

cases.Case (English): A 48-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presents to the emergency room with altered mental status over the last several hours. Preliminary laboratory studies are notable for a serum ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL, and INR of 6.8. Her husband reports that she has consistently been taking pain medications and started taking additional 500 mg acetaminophen pills several days ago for lower back pain. Further history reveals a medication list with multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations.

cases.Case (English): A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 65 y/o m, cannot open mouth, contraction of muscles causing painful spasms for minutes, sweating, tachycardia, cut hand while gardening, did not get tetanus shot
cases.Topic and source: Tetanus · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Topic and source: COPD flare (milder) · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 30 y/o f, 2 day fever, cough, headache, weakness, did not get flu shot
cases.Topic and source: Influenza · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 16 y/o f, 1 week Hx of fever, sore throat, fatigue, difficulty swallowing, fever, enlarged lymph nodes, exudates, macular rash on trunk/arms
cases.Topic and source: Mononucleosis · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 40-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 2-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain. He describes the pain as a dull, gnawing ache. The pain sometimes wakes him at night, is relieved by food and drinking milk, and is helped partially by ranitidine. He had a similar but milder episode about 5 years ago, which was treated with omeprazole. Physical examination reveals a fit, apparently healthy man in no distress. The only abnormal finding is mild epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 40 y/o m, 2 month Hx of intermittent upper abdominal pain, dulling and gnawing ache, wakes at night and is relieved by food/drinking milk/ranitidine, prior episode 5 yrs ago
cases.Topic and source: Peptic Ulcer Disease · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 6-year-old boy with a medical history significant for mild persistent asthma is brought to the clinic by his mother with a history of a 5-day cough. His mother reports that the child's fever continues to be elevated despite acetaminophen therapy. He has missed school for the past 3 days and he has a classmate sick with pneumonia. The mother reports that the appetite is good for the child. His cough produced yellowish sputum at home. His vitals at the clinic are: respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, heart rate 80 beats/min, and temperature 101.6°F (38.7°C). He appears in no respiratory distress. His lung examination reveals bilateral rales and occasional wheeze. CXR reveals lobar infiltrates without pleural effusions.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 6 y/o m, Hx of asthma, 5 days cough, fever, appetite good, yellow sputum, t 101.6
cases.Topic and source: Pneumonia · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 14 y/o m, nausea, vomiting, non-bloody diarrhea, mild abdominal cramps (T=100.1), mild abdominal tenderness, diarrhea after attending a picnic and eating undercooked chicken,
cases.Topic and source: Salmonella · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 77 y/o m, 5 day burning and aching on right side of chest, erythema, maculopapular rash, headache, malaise, rash progressed to clear vesicles after 3-5 days
cases.Topic and source: Shingles · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 26-year-old female newly wed presents complaining of painful urination, feeling of urgent need to urinate, and more frequent urination for 2 days. She denies any fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, vaginal discharge, or vaginal pruritus.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 26 y/o f, painful urination, urgent need to urinate, more frequent urination for 2 days, sexually active; no fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, vaginal discharge, vaginal pruritus
cases.Topic and source: Urinary tract infection · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 65-year-old woman presents with a chief complaint of dizziness. She describes it as a sudden and severe spinning sensation precipitated by rolling over in bed onto her right side. Symptoms typically last <30 seconds. They have occurred nightly over the last month and occasionally during the day when she tilts her head back to look upward. She describes no precipitating event prior to onset and no associated hearing loss, tinnitus, or other neurologic symptoms. Otologic and neurologic examinations are normal except for the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which is negative on the left but strongly positive on the right side.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 65 y/o f, dizziness, sudden onset, recurrent, lasts <30 sec, consistent trigger, no hearing loss, ringing in ears, muscle weakness, loss of sensation
cases.Topic and source: Vertigo · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 34-year-old woman with no known underlying lung disease 12-day history of cough. She initially had nasal congestion and a mild sore throat, but now her symptoms are all related to a productive cough without paroxysms. She denies any sick contacts. On physical examination she is not in respiratory distress and is afebrile with normal vital signs. No signs of URI are noted. Scattered wheezes are present diffusely on lung auscultation.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 34 y/o f, 12 day cough, initial nasal congestion and sore throat, cough, no fever
cases.Topic and source: Acute bronchitis · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 61 y/o f, 4 day cough, yellow sputum, rhinorrhea, fever (resolved)
cases.Topic and source: Acute bronchitis · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history presents 3 days after developing a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today. He has watery discharge from both eyes and they are stuck shut in the morning. He reports recent upper respiratory symptoms and that several children at his day camp recently had pink eye. He denies significant pain or light sensitivity and does not wear contact lenses. On examination, his pupils are equal and reactive and he has a right-sided, tender preauricular lymph node. Penlight examination does not reveal any corneal opacity.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 14 y/o m, 3 days red, irritated eye (spread from right to left), discharge, URI symptoms, no pain or light sensitivity
cases.Topic and source: Acute conjunctivitis · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): Mr. E is a 26 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat. He has been afebrile. His physical examination is normal, except for some pharyngeal erythema. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 26 y/o m, 2 day sore throat, headache, cough, no fever
cases.Topic and source: Acute pharyngitis · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse during the spring season. On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. He remembers that his mother told him at some point that he used to have eczema in infancy.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 22 y/o m, 5 year Hx of nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal itching worse during spring season, eye itching, redness, tearing, palate and throat itching, Hx of eczema in infancy
cases.Topic and source: Allergic rhinitis · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 38-year-old man with no significant history of back pain developed acute LBP when lifting boxes 2 weeks ago. The pain is aching in nature, located in the left lumbar area, and associated with spasms. He describes previous similar episodes several years ago, which resolved without seeing a doctor. He denies any leg pain or weakness. He also denies fevers, chills, weight loss, and recent infections. Over-the-counter ibuprofen has helped somewhat, but he has taken it only twice a day for the past 3 days because he does not want to become dependent on painkillers. On examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and extension secondary to pain, but a neurologic exam is unremarkable.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 38 y/o m, acute low back pain after lifting, no leg pain or weakness, no fevers, chills, weight loss, or recent infections
cases.Topic and source: Back pain · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 9 y/o m, bee sting, swollen and tender upper lip; no tongue swelling, drooling, stridor, rash, or other complaints
cases.Topic and source: Bee sting without anaphylaxis · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 17-year-old male student presents with recurrent mouth ulceration since his early schooldays. He has no respiratory, anogenital, gastrointestinal, eye, or skin lesions. His mother had a similar history as a teenager. The social history includes no tobacco use and virtually no alcohol consumption. He has no history of recent drug or medication ingestion. Extraoral exam reveals no significant abnormalities and specifically no pyrexia; no cervical lymph node enlargement; nor cranial nerve, salivary, or temporomandibular joint abnormalities. Oral exam reveals a well-restored dentition and there is no clinical evidence of periodontal-attachment loss or pocketing. He has five 4 mm round ulcers with inflammatory haloes in his buccal mucosae.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 17 y/o m with recurrent mouth ulceration for year, no respiratory, anogenital, gastrointestinal, eye, or skin lesions, mother has similar Hx, no Hx of recent drugs or medication
cases.Topic and source: Canker sore · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): Consider a 40-year-old, monogamous, married woman who calls to report a 2-day history of vaginal itching and thick white discharge. She has no abdominal pain or fever. (in study 50% recommended physician visit)
cases.Symptoms / flags: 40 y/o f, 2 day vaginal itching, thick white discharge, no abdominal pain or fever
cases.Topic and source: Candidal yeast infection · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 5 mo m, difficulty/delay in passing hard stools, strains for hours, may miss a day, screams when passes stool and occasional spots of blood, weaned from breastmilk to cows' milk, now feeding normally
cases.Topic and source: Constipation · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 12-year-old female presents with dry, itchy skin that involves the flexures in front of her elbows, behind her knees, and in front of her ankles. Her cheeks also have patches of dry, scaly skin. She has symptoms of hay fever and has recently been diagnosed with egg and milk allergy. She has a brother with asthma and an uncle and several cousins who have been diagnosed with eczema.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 12 y/o f, dry, itchy skin in front of elbows, behind knees, in front of ankles, cheeks have patches of dry, scaly skin, symptoms of hay fever, egg and milk allergy, brother has asthma and uncle and cousins have eczema
cases.Topic and source: Eczema · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 30-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen right eye for the past day. He reports minor pain on palpation of the eyelid and denies any history of trauma, crusting, or change in vision. He has no history of allergies or any eye conditions and denies the use of any new soaps, lotions, or creams. On exam, he has localized tenderness to palpation and erythema on the midline of the lower eyelid near the lid margin. The remainder of the physical exam, including the globe, is normal.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 30 y/o m, painful, swollen right eye for past day, no Hx of trauma, crusting, change in vision, allergies, or eye conditions, localized tenderness, erythema (redness)
cases.Topic and source: Stye · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): Mr. R. is a 56 year-old man who presents to you with 6 days of non-productive cough, nasal congestion, and green nasal discharge. He has had intermittent fevers as high as 100.8. His physical examination is normal except for rhinorrhea. He is otherwise healthy, except for chronic osteoarthritis of the right knee. He has no drug allergies.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 56 y/o m, 6 day cough, nasal congestion, green nasal discharge, fever (100.8), rhinorrhea
cases.Topic and source: Viral upper respiratory illness (56 y) · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): A 30-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of runny nose and sore throat. He feels hot and sweaty, has a mild headache, is coughing up clear sputum and complains of muscle aches. He would like antibiotics as he was prescribed them last year when he had a similar condition. On examination, he is afebrile, has a normal pulse, a slightly inflamed pharynx and nontender cervical lymphadenopathy. There is no neck stiffness and his chest is clear. He has tried over-the-counter cough medications, but has not found these helpful. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day.
cases.Symptoms / flags: 30 y/o m, 2 day HX of runny nose, sore throat, hot, sweaty, mild headache, cough with clear sputum, muscle aches, no fever or neck stiffness
cases.Topic and source: Viral upper respiratory illness (30 y) · adult · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

cases.Case (English): Elizabeth's 2-year-old son has a fever and vomited twice. Elizabeth worries about dehydration, so she gives Jack a sippy cup of apple juice. He immediately vomits up the juice. Elizabeth debates what to do next. Should she try to reach Jack's pediatrician or should she take Jack to the ED? Instead, she calls her triage nurse line. Temperature = 100.5
cases.Symptoms / flags: 2 y/o m, low grade fever (T = 100.5), vomited twice, vomits up juice
cases.Topic and source: Vomiting · paediatric · Semigran et al., BMJ 2015 (CC BY-NC 4.0)

levels.Meaning on the spacecraft: Review within 24 hours, or at the next scheduled medical conference with Earth.
Self-care with the medical kit, monitor and reassess; escalate if worse.
Data missing or unreliable: measure again and repeat. The app does not guess.
